newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Bildt says troops needed in Bosnia past 1998.
newsitem.headline: Bildt says troops needed in Bosnia past 1998.

text.p: International envoy to Bosnia Carl Bildt said on Friday the Western allies should keep a multi-national peace force in the Balkan country beyond the June 1998 deadline for troop withdrawal.
Bildt, speaking to reporters at a NATO meeting in Portugal, said the remaining time was not enough for the 30,000-strong NATO-led force to complete the task of securing a lasting peace in Bosnia.
"I think forces will still be needed on the ground," Bildt said. But he declined to say how many troops would be required or how much longer they would have to stay.

Bildt, who is due to step down soon as the international community's High Representative in Bosnia, said he had consistently pointed to "a need for a security component of the overall mission after June 1998."
"We must not allow a security vacuum to develop," he said.

Bildt's assertion comes amid increasing concern about the faltering Bosnian peace process. Some NATO ministers attending the Sintra meeting have suggested the troop withdrawal deadline should be extended, but U.S. officials have so far resisted the idea.
NATO officials on Friday planned to step up pressure on Bosnian leaders to comply with the 1995 Dayton peace accords, including a requirement to turn over indicted war criminals for prosecution.
Ministers were expected to begin tightening the screws when the three members of Bosnia's revolving presidency meet in Sintra with a mulit-national peacekeeping council.
Bildt said the allies would make specific demands of the Bosnian leadership and attach deadlines for fulfilling them.
Under the Dayton agreement, Bosnia is supposed to be a single state comprising autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories.

But the inter-ethnic central cabinet and presidency have failed to carry out most of the major peace provisions. Few refugees have been able to return to their homes, and the delivery of reconstruction aid has been held up by disputes among rival ethnic leaders.
